A1.justification: Despite the changed title, both PDFs describe the same block-sparse attention work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction, pose-estimation, runtime, and ablation results for sparse VGGT and π3 in Section 5 and the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds MapAnything evaluations, sparse-attention comparisons, and long-trajectory ScanNet experiments.

M1.justification: Both versions use pooled query/key similarities, combined top-k and CDF block selection, and dense interactions involving special tokens. V2 applies this procedure to MapAnything and clarifies differences from SpargeAttention without documenting a changed algorithm or training objective.

E1.justification: The named datasets and core pose-estimation and pointmap tasks are retained; 7Scenes, NRGBD, TUM, and ScanNet already had results in v1. V2 Appendix B adds a distinct scenario spanning complete, longer and more complex ScanNet trajectories, providing a bounded expansion of test coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 10 adds evaluated SpargeAttention variants, random masking, and CDF-only controls. Figure 7 also adds MapAnything and explicit dense-model reference comparisons. The SeerAttention-style learned-projection experiment already existed in v1 and is retained, rather than newly introduced.

E3.justification: The new ScanNet experiment evaluates 50 sequences with 100, 300, 500, and 1000 frames evenly sampled across complete trajectories. V2 also introduces MapAnything configurations and masking controls explicitly excluding Hilbert permutation. Tanks & Temples retains only 50/100/200-frame configurations, dropping 25-frame and full-length evaluations, and revises its reported sparsity-parameter grid. These are substantial evaluation-design changes.

E4.justification: V2 adds comparisons testing combined thresholding against CDF-only and random selection, MapAnything layer-skipping experiments, and analyses of its attention statistics. Additional reconstruction and trajectory examples examine behavior under high sparsity. V1's special-token, learned-projection, and VGGT layer-skipping ablations remain, with renumbering and expanded discussion.

E5.justification: V2 Figure 4 explicitly identifies the existing shaded bands as standard deviations and the solid curves as means over tokens; v1 displayed these bands without that explanation. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the benchmark results.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive MapAnything and full-trajectory ScanNet results, revises DTU and Tanks & Temples values, and updates effective sparsity values in retained tables. For example, the nominal 10%, CDF 0.970 VGGT DTU row changes Acc from 1.196 to 1.075 and N.C. from 0.679 to 0.613. Identical underlying settings are not established, so these are reported revisions rather than demonstrated same-setting gains. V1's absolute-runtime table and 25-frame/full-length Tanks results are removed.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix A adds model-level FLOP derivations, equations (3)–(7), counting assumptions and exclusions, and theoretical speed-up estimates in Table A-1. V1 contained only the simpler asymptotic speed-up argument. The addition is substantial, although its dense-attention sparsity convention is inconsistent and equation (6) omits the stated global-layer multiplicity.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden demonstrated applicability from VGGT and π3 to include MapAnything. The headline acceleration changes from up to 4× to more than 3×, explicitly described as end-to-end in the introduction. The central contributions of attention analysis, training-free sparsification, and preserving task performance remain.

C2.justification: V2 introduces architecture-dependent explanations: MapAnything's reliance on later layers is linked to predicting poses from patch tokens, and its attention statistics are linked to its single special token. It also attributes apparent ETH3D improvements to randomness, discusses degradation on harder full trajectories, and qualifies MapAnything timing measurements because of preprocessing and postprocessing. These substantially expand mechanisms and limitations beyond v1.

D1.justification: V2 adds a project-page link, documents the existing TUM/ScanNet 90-frame, stride-3 sampling, and specifies sampling and controls for new experiments. It removes v1's explicit ten-random-frame pointmap sampling statement and the Tanks timing table's resolution disclosure. The learned-projection training hyperparameters, block sizes, hardware, and training time are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 substantially expands positioning against sparse attention, low-rank approximations, spatial/temporal attention, and weight pruning. Added works include Scatterbrain, MInference, FlexPrefill, MoBA, and SparseGPT, alongside MapAnything elsewhere. V2 more precisely distinguishes its kernel reuse and block selection from SpargeAttention and learned approaches such as SeerAttention.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, rewrites the abstract, polishes terminology and grammar, expands related-work explanations, and adds an explicit ablation subsection. The appendices are reorganized around new theory and long-sequence sections. Most existing method and attention-analysis prose retains its original structure and narrative.

P2.justification: V2 substantially revises the visual presentation: Figure 2 becomes compact, Figure 7 gains model series and reference lines, Figure 8 replaces examples and sparsity levels, and Figure 9 changes its panels and displayed metric from RRA@5 to AUC@30, already tabulated in v1. Table 1 is removed, Figure 10 is added, and appendix plots and table structures expand for the new analyses and model.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the method's design, generality, and scalability through direct sparse-attention controls, an architecturally different model, and complete-trajectory ScanNet evaluation. These address important validation gaps in v1, while the ETH3D randomness qualification improves interpretation. The gains are tempered by removal of the absolute-runtime table and inconsistencies in the new FLOP derivation, which weaken timing transparency and theoretical rigor. Nevertheless, the central empirical case is substantially better supported.
